RobustRLlib: A Unified Library and Benchmark for Robust Reinforcement Learning Algorithms

Xi Chen22footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: JHU    Fengqi Hu11footnotemark: 1 22footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: JHU    Zeyu Shen11footnotemark: 1 33footnotemark: 3 Affiliation: JHU    Jiaying Xu55footnotemark: 5 Affiliation: UCSD    Shangding Gu66footnotemark: 6 Affiliation: UC Berkeley    Pan Xu77footnotemark: 7 Affiliation: Duke    Anqi Liu22footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: JHU    Laixi Shi44footnotemark: 4 Affiliation: JHU
October 23, 2026
Abstract

Robust reinforcement learning (RL) is critical for reliable real-world deployment, where policies may fail under diverse shifts and disruptions. Existing robust RL algorithms offer a rich set of mechanisms and principles, yet two major barriers limit their broader potential: limited algorithm reusability and an unclear empirical capability boundary. We introduce RobustRLlib, an algorithm-centric library and benchmark that addresses both challenges. It integrates 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms under a unified interface for substantially improved reusability, together with an enhanced evaluation platform spanning diverse real-world shifts and advanced humanoid and vision-language-action tasks. Systematic evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations provides an up-to-date capability map of current robust RL algorithms, revealing where they remain effective and where substantial robustness gaps persist. As an open-source, user-friendly platform, RobustRLlib offers a reproducible and extensible codebase for applying existing methods to new problems and developing new robust RL algorithms. The code and tutorial are available at https://robustrl-lib.github.io.

Keywords: Robust RL, benchmark, algorithm library, distribution shift, sim-to-real transfer

1 Introduction

Despite remarkable advances in reinforcement learning (RL), its real-world deployment remains limited by robustness and safety concerns, particularly in high-stakes domains such as autonomous driving (Ding et al., 2023b), clinical trials (Liu et al., 2015), robotics (Li et al., 2021), and semiconductor manufacturing (Kozak et al., 2023). Policies trained in idealized environments can easily fail under distribution shifts or disruptions affecting various stages of the interaction, such as observations (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2021; Xiong et al., 2022), actions (Huang et al., 2017), or environment dynamics (Iyengar, 2005; Pinto et al., 2017), induced by diverse factors such as sim-to-real gaps (Pinto et al., 2017), model uncertainty (Bertsimas et al., 2019), noise, or adversarial attacks (Zhang et al., 2020; Klopp et al., 2017; Mahmood et al., 2018).

Robust RL therefore aims to develop policies that remain reliable under diverse types of disruptions and shifts, or their combinations in real-world scenarios (Bertsimas et al., 2019; Tversky and Kahneman, 1974; Arthur, 1991). A broad range of robust RL algorithms has shown strong performance in their specific type of disrupted application scenarios. More importantly, existing methods provide a rich set of robustness mechanisms and principles, including adversarial training (Pinto et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021; Rigter et al., 2022), dynamics randomization (Peng et al., 2018), robust value updates (Yang et al., 2022; Panaganti et al., 2022), and data augmentation (Yu et al., 2020b; Lu et al., 2023; Ding et al., 2024), offering substantial promise across a far broader range of applications and shift scenarios.

However, realizing this broader potential faces two fundamental barriers: algorithm reusability and systematic characterization of the capability boundary. First, existing robust RL algorithms are fragmented across separate implementations and training pipelines, lacking a unified library or interface through which practitioners can readily try and compare a broad collection of robust RL methods on a new application. Second, the empirical capability boundary of current robust RL remains unclear: for a given application and distribution shift, we lack a systematic understanding of how well existing methods perform, when they remain effective, and where they fail. This is largely because the methods are typically evaluated in distinct environments and shift scenarios, making cross-method comparison difficult and performance beyond their original settings poorly understood.

To address these two gaps, we introduce RobustRLlib, an algorithm-centric robust RL benchmark that brings together (1) a robust RL method library with reusable implementations to substantially lower the barrier to applying existing methods to new problems, and (2) a comprehensive evaluation pipeline across tasks and diverse real-world shift scenarios. Complementing existing robust RL benchmarks that primarily focus on developing evaluation tasks and shift scenarios (Dulac-Arnold et al., 2020; Zouitine et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2025), RobustRLlib focuses on making robust RL algorithms systematically accessible, comparable, and extensible, while providing a broader evaluation framework (Comparison in Appendix A.1). Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    A robust RL algorithm library. We integrate existing 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms, understanding and systematically organizing them by their learning methods, intended target shifts, and base algorithms for applicators’ easy reference. It provides a reusable foundation for applying existing methods to new applications and developing new robust RL algorithms.

  • •

    An enhanced evaluation platform. Our extensible disruptor toolbox covers a broad range of distribution shifts, including MDP-element shifts in observations, actions, dynamics, and reward/cost, as well as control-loop latency and task-semantic shifts. It supports diverse shift modes, including stochastic, adversarial, and parametric perturbations with non-stationary schedules, enabling both isolated and compound-shift evaluation. The same disruptor interface further extends to massively parallel training in Isaac Lab (Mittal et al., 2025) and advanced vision–language–action (VLA) robotic tasks (Intelligence et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026).

  • •

    An up-to-date capability map of robust RL algorithms. Evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations reveals that robust methods outperform standard references on average, but both groups deteriorate markedly as shifts intensify. A method’s claimed target shift does not reliably predict its empirical strengths, gains vary across tasks and shift sources, with online methods showing larger incremental effects than offline ones. By connecting diverse algorithm features to their measured strengths, this map provides guidance for designing robust RL methods for deployment shifts.

2 Related Work

Robust RL problems under diverse deployment shifts.

Robust RL addresses deployment shifts affecting different components and stages of the agent–environment interaction, and prior work can be categorized accordingly. Zhang et al. (2020); Zhang et al. (2021); Oikarinen et al. (2021) address observation shift, which perturbs policy inputs through sensing errors or external attacks. Tessler et al. (2019); Tan et al. (2020) address action shift, which perturbs or replaces executed actions. Dynamics shift, involving uncertainty in or changes to the transition kernel, is addressed either by optimizing worst-case performance over ambiguity sets (Nilim and El Ghaoui, 2005; Iyengar, 2005; Xu and Mannor, 2010; Wiesemann et al., 2013; Goyal and Grand-Clement, 2023; Shi et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2024; Shi and Chi, 2024) or by introducing random or adversarial perturbations to physical parameters and external forces (Rajeswaran et al., 2016; Peng et al., 2018; Pinto et al., 2017; Mankowitz et al., 2019). Queeney and Benosman (2023); Ma et al. (2019) address reward and cost shifts through constraint-aware learning, and reward-poisoning analysis. Beyond these MDP components, Bouteiller et al. (2021); Peng et al. (2018); Tan et al. (2018) address latency shift, involving delays or irregularities in observation and action timing. Tobin et al. (2017); Ding et al. (2023a) address semantic shift, involving changes in appearance or task-relevant relationships among visual cues, objects, and goals. In practice, real-world scenarios may involve multiple shifts, such as changes in dynamics parameters, process noise, and observation noise (Mandlekar et al., 2017), or non-stationary shifts that evolve during deployment (Lecarpentier and Rachelson, 2019). Since robustness to one shift does not necessarily extend to others or their combinations, this motivates developing algorithms for co-occurring shifts and evaluating them under a unified framework.

Robust RL algorithm taxonomy.

Robust RL algorithms promote robustness through two main approaches: modifying the learning objective or algorithm (learner-centric) and modifying the training data distribution (data-centric). For robust online RL, learner-centric methods seek robust policies through optimization against an adversary (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021), worst-case robust value objectives (Liang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024), smoothing the policy over perturbed observations (Sun et al., 2024), or causal-inspired data augmentation to handle spurious correlated shifted scenarios (Ding et al., 2023a). Data-centric methods can collect trajectories by interacting with shifted environments through physical parameter randomization (Peng et al., 2018), model ensembles (Rajeswaran et al., 2016; Mankowitz et al., 2019; Tanabe et al., 2022), or by applying adversarial disturbances (Pinto et al., 2017). For robust offline RL, learner-centric methods address model uncertainty and limited data coverage through robust Bellman updates over an uncertainty set of transitions (Panaganti et al., 2022; Blanchet et al., 2023; Panaganti et al., 2023), and mitigate value overestimation by smoothness regularization over perturbed states (Yang et al., 2022). Data-centric methods instead augment or reweight fixed datasets by generating samples from adversarial environments (Rigter et al., 2022; Bhardwaj et al., 2023), mixing diffusion-generated synthetic data with real data (Lu et al., 2023), or downweighting corrupted samples (Yang et al., 2024). In particular, generative-model methods, as a data-centric subfamily, learn dynamics models from offline data and generates plausible future transitions or multi-step trajectories for robust policy learning (Ding et al., 2024; Berdica et al., 2024; Foffano et al., 2026). Furthermore, robust safe RL extends robust policy learning to jointly maintain task performance and satisfy cost constraints under uncertainty (Liu et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Queeney and Benosman, 2023). In this work, RobustRLlib integrates 17 representative algorithms spanning robust online, offline, and safe RL, systematically organizes them by algorithm features, and evaluates them across diverse shift sources and modes under a unified protocol. It provides a reusable foundation for applying existing methods to new applications and developing new robust RL algorithms.

Related RL benchmarks.

Existing RL benchmarks can be broadly categorized into data-oriented benchmarks, which primarily provide fixed datasets for algorithm development (Fu et al., 2020; Gulcehre et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2022); task-oriented benchmarks, which offer standardized tasks and environments for developing and evaluating RL algorithms, ranging from continuous control to advanced robotics (Duan et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2020a; Sferrazza et al., 2024; Ji et al., 2023; Pumacay et al., 2024); and algorithm-oriented libraries and benchmarks, which provide reproducible implementations, training infrastructure, and pipelines for existing RL algorithms, serving as a foundation for downstream applications, fair comparisons, and further algorithm development (Liang et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2023; Raffin et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2022; Weng et al., 2022). In particular, for robust RL, closely related task-oriented benchmarks include RRLS, which focuses on continuous control (Zouitine et al., 2024), and Robust-Gymnasium, which covers a broader range of control and robotics tasks (Gu et al., 2025). Complementing these efforts, this work introduces RobustRLlib, the first unified algorithm-oriented library and benchmark for robust RL. It provides a reusable foundation for applying existing methods to new applications and developing new robust RL algorithms, while enabling easy comparisons with existing methods. In addition, RobustRLlib extends the considered deployment shifts to include latency and semantic shifts, and expands evaluation to advanced high-dimensional robotic tasks. There exist other benchmarks that address related settings, such as off-dynamics transfer, real-world operating stressors, and adversarial robustness (Lyu et al., 2024; Dulac-Arnold et al., 2020; Mohan et al., 2026).

Sim-to-real gap in robotics.

The sim-to-real gap is a longstanding challenge in robotics, where mismatches between simulation and real-world hardware can substantially degrade the performance of policies trained in simulation. Prior work addresses this gap through various approaches, including dynamics randomization (Peng et al., 2018; Andrychowicz et al., 2020), actuator and latency modeling (Tan et al., 2018), and online adaptation to changing dynamics (Kumar et al., 2021). These considerations have been explored in whole-body humanoid control (Gu et al., 2024; He et al., 2024), safety-critical robotics (As et al., 2026), real-time VLA policies that overlap execution and inference (Black et al., 2026), and demonstration-driven policies for contact-rich manipulation (Sharma et al., 2026). However, many existing approaches are task-specific and address particular sources of sim-to-real mismatch. In this work, we provide a unified robust RL algorithm library with 17 representative algorithms covering diverse tasks and sim-to-real gaps. These algorithms and their underlying design principles have the potential to support broader robotics applications while reducing manual iteration before hardware deployment.

3 RobustRLlib: An Algorithm-Centric Robust RL Benchmark

RobustRLlib is organized around algorithm attribution: it records how a robust RL method changes learning, which shift the method claims to address, and which base algorithm realizes the method. The disruptor toolbox then instantiates the claimed target shift independently of the base learner, while the evaluation platform measures both common robustness and method-specific specialization. This separation makes each result traceable to an algorithmic feature and an evaluation condition rather than treating robust RL as a single undifferentiated class.

Markov decision processes (MDP).

We consider a finite-horizon MDP ℳ0=(𝒮,𝒜,T,P0,r0)\mathcal{M}_{0}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,P_{0},r_{0}), where 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒜\mathcal{A} are the state and action spaces, TT is the horizon, and P0P_{0} and r0r_{0} denote the nominal transition kernel and reward function. At time tt, the policy selects at∼πt(⋅∣st)a_{t}\sim\pi_{t}(\cdot\mid s_{t}), receives reward r0,t​(st,at)r_{0,t}(s_{t},a_{t}), and the environment transitions according to st+1∼P0,t(⋅∣st,at)s_{t+1}\sim P_{0,t}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}). Classical robust MDPs replace the nominal transition model P0P_{0} with a shift set 𝒫\mathcal{P} and seek a policy with high worst-case return (Iyengar, 2005; Nilim and El Ghaoui, 2005):

max⁡infP∈𝒫π⁡J⁡(π,P,r0),J⁡(π,P,r0)=𝔼π,P​[∑t=1Tr0,t​(st,at)].\max_{\pi}\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}}J(\pi;P,r_{0}),\qquad J(\pi;P,r_{0})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi,P}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{0,t}(s_{t},a_{t})\right]. (1)

For safety-constrained tasks, we augment the MDP with a cost function c={ct}t=1Tc=\{c_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} and a budget dd, requiring 𝔼π,P​[∑t=1Tct​(st,at)]≤d\mathbb{E}_{\pi,P}[\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}(s_{t},a_{t})]\leq d in addition to maximizing task return. This cost interface is retained when shift is introduced, allowing robustness and safety to be evaluated jointly.

3.1 Robust RL algorithm library construction

The library has three tracks: offline RL learns from fixed data, online RL learns through continued environment interaction, and safe RL adds cost constraints, including robust-safe methods implemented here in the online setting. Within the offline and online tracks, robustness primarily enters through two routes: learner-centric methods change how experience is interpreted or optimized, while data-centric and environment-centric methods change the distribution available for learning. Table 1 summarizes each method’s feature, target shift, and base algorithm.

3.1.1 Robust offline RL algorithms

Offline RL learns from a fixed dataset without environment interaction, making limited data coverage and optimistic value estimates for unsupported actions central challenges. Robust offline RL must also maintain performance under distribution shift. We therefore group its methods by how they address these challenges: learner-centric methods modify the objective or update, whereas data-centric methods reshape the training distribution, including through data augmentation or generative models. As standard RL baselines, IQL (Kostrikov et al., 2021) and TD3+BC (Fujimoto and Gu, 2021) learn directly from logged transitions; MOPO (Yu et al., 2020b) adds model rollouts, and SynthER (Lu et al., 2023) adds diffusion-generated datasets.

Learner-centric methods.

These methods make policy learning less sensitive to uncertain transitions or perturbed observations by changing the value target or policy update.

  • •

    RFQI: worst-case Bellman update. RFQI (Panaganti et al., 2022) replaces the nominal fitted-QQ target with a worst-case backup over transition ambiguity.

  • •

    RORL: local policy and value smoothing. RORL (Yang et al., 2022) combines pessimistic bootstrapping with smoothing around states to stabilize predictions under observation perturbations.

  • •

    ATLA: observation adversary. The offline ATLA adaptation (Zhang et al., 2021) trains an observation adversary alongside standard base algorithm, exposing policy updates to adverse inputs.

Data-centric methods.

These methods expand the experience available to the base learner through counterfactual transitions or model-generated rollouts.

  • •

    RSC: causal counterfactual rewrite. The offline RSC (Ding et al., 2023a) adaptation rewrites samples using an inferred causal mask to weaken spurious semantic correlations.

  • •

    RAMBO: adversarial model rollouts. RAMBO (Rigter et al., 2022) branches short synthetic rollouts from dataset states and adjusts its dynamics model adversarially within a data-fit constraint.

Generative model methods.

These data-centric methods learn conditional models of transition dynamics and use generated next states or multi-step futures in policy learning, which potentially improve robustness under dynamics shifts. SynthER is excluded from this family because it models the distribution of logged transitions to enlarge the dataset rather than modeling dynamics for policy learning.

  • •

    ROMB: maximin model ensemble. ROMB (Chen et al., 2025) optimizes against adverse transitions represented by an ensemble of learned models.

  • •

    FWM: flow-generated multi-step targets. FWM uses flow-matching to replace diffusion world model (Ding et al., 2024) and samples future trajectories to construct multi-step critic targets.

  • •

    PLR-PVL: worst-case world model selection. PLR-PVL (Berdica et al., 2024) searches a flow-model ensemble for adverse plausible futures during policy learning.

3.1.2 Robust online RL algorithms

Online robust RL methods preserve continued interaction with the environment but differ in where robustness enters training. We distinguish two primary routes. Learner-centric methods modify the policy input and learning objective while retaining the nominal physical transition law. Environment-centric methods instead interact with deliberately perturbed environments to collect training rollouts. Whether a method updates on-policy or off-policy remains an important implementation choice, so we record it through the base algorithm. PPO (Schulman et al., 2017), TRPO (Schulman et al., 2015) and SAC (Haarnoja et al., 2018) serve as the standard base algorithms in our experiments.

Learner-centric methods.

These methods train the policy to make stable decisions using adversarial observations, local regularization, or causal counterfactual experience.

  • •

    ATLA: observation adversary. ATLA (Zhang et al., 2021) alternates updates between the policy and a learned adversary that perturbs its observations.

  • •

    ATLA-SA: state-adversarial regularization. ATLA-SA (Zhang et al., 2021) adds recurrent history and SA-MDP regularization to stabilize decisions under perturbed observations.

  • •

    RSC: causal counterfactual replay. RSC (Ding et al., 2023a) infers causal dependencies and rewrites experience counterfactually to reduce reliance on spurious semantic features.

Environment-centric methods.

These methods build robustness through training trajectories generated under varied physical environments or external disturbances.

  • •

    RARL: external force adversary. RARL (Pinto et al., 2017) perturbs the environment with bounded forces selected by an adaptive adversary. The protagonist and adversary train in a two-player game, concentrating experience on the policy’s current vulnerabilities.

  • •

    DR: domain randomization. DR (Peng et al., 2018) samples physical parameters across training episodes, exposing the policy to a prescribed envelope of transition dynamics.

3.1.3 Robust safe RL algorithms

Robust safe RL methods seek to maximize worst-case expected return while ensuring cost-constraint satisfaction across a prescribed dynamics uncertainty set.

  • •

    RAMU: risk-sensitive reward and cost targets. RAMU (Queeney and Benosman, 2023) applies risk measures over transition-model uncertainty to both reward and cost Bellman targets.

  • •

    SPiDR: robust safety via penalized costs. SPiDR (As et al., 2026) measures disagreement among next-state predictions from domain-randomized models and penalizes uncertain safety outcomes.

3.2 Expandable disruptor toolbox

Robust RL preserves the underlying task objective of standard RL by maximizing cumulative return but extends the single nominal MDP into a family of robust MDP with different types of shifts. These shifts intervene in different components of the agent–environment interaction, such as observations, actions, transition dynamics, rewards or costs, latency, and task semantics. The resulting robust RL problem therefore seeks a policy that performs reliably across these shifted interaction conditions.

3.2.1 Shift sources

We classify a shift by where it enters the agent–environment interaction. The first four sources act directly on components of the MDP interface (Figure 2(a)); latency (Figure 2(b)) and semantics (Figure 2(c)) then capture deployment factors that are not represented cleanly by a single nominal MDP component. Given xt=(st,a~t)x_{t}=(s_{t},\tilde{a}_{t}) and yt=(st,a~t,st+1)y_{t}=(s_{t},\tilde{a}_{t},s_{t+1}), we expose the six shift sources as below:

  • •

    Dynamic shift. Changes the environment response under the same state and executed action, st+1∼Pθp(⋅∣xt)s_{t+1}\sim P_{\theta^{p}}(\cdot\mid x_{t}), where θp\theta^{p} specifies physical-parameter changes, external disturbances, and latent process noise. Its operators cover physical changes including internal dynamics such as morphology, friction, gravity and external disturbance such as wind, external pushes, and latent noise. These variations represent physical mismatch and motivate dynamics randomization for sim-to-real control (Peng et al., 2018).

  • •

    Observation shift. Changes the information available to the policy, o~t∼Oθo(⋅∣st)\tilde{o}_{t}\sim O_{\theta^{o}}(\cdot\mid s_{t}) and at∼π(⋅∣o~t)a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid\tilde{o}_{t}), where θo\theta^{o} specifies the perturbation applied to the policy observation. It represents sensor noise, bias, missing or imperfect feedback, and bounded observation attacks (Dulac-Arnold et al., 2020).

  • •

    Action shift. Changes the command that reaches the plant, a~t∼Aθa(⋅∣st,at)\tilde{a}_{t}\sim A_{\theta^{a}}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}), where θa\theta^{a} specifies how the intended action is altered before execution. It captures execution noise, calibration error, saturation, opposition, and other actuator-side distortions (Tessler et al., 2019).

  • •

    Reward/cost shift. Changes the feedback used for task learning or safety evaluation, r~t∼Rθr(⋅∣yt)\tilde{r}_{t}\sim R_{\theta^{r}}(\cdot\mid y_{t}) and c~t∼Cθc(⋅∣yt)\tilde{c}_{t}\sim C_{\theta^{c}}(\cdot\mid y_{t}), where θr​c=(θr,θc)\theta^{rc}=(\theta^{r},\theta^{c}) specifies the reward and cost perturbations. It represents noisy or biased supervision while keeping the underlying transition explicit.

  • •

    Latency shift. Captures deployment-time mismatch in the timing of sensing, action execution, control, and VLA inference delay (Dulac-Arnold et al., 2020; Bouteiller et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2018). We treat latency as a composable deployment-shift source within this unified robust RL evaluation framework. Specifically, we expose observation delay, action delay, and control-period variation through o~t=ℐ(ℋt,t−δo),a~t=at−δa,st+1∼P0(κt)(⋅∣st,a~t)\tilde{o}_{t}=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{H}_{t},t-\delta_{o}),\tilde{a}_{t}=a_{t-\delta_{a}},s_{t+1}\sim P_{0}^{(\kappa_{t})}(\cdot\mid s_{t},\tilde{a}_{t}), capturing delayed sensing, delayed execution, and variable control rates, respectively. Implementation details are provided in Appendix A.2.1.

  • •

    Semantic shift. Changes task-relevant scenes or structures rather than merely adding task-agnostic noise. Such shifts can be represented as ot∼Oθz(⋅∣st),st+1∼Pθz(⋅∣xt),(rt,ct)∼(Rθz,Cθz)(⋅∣yt)o_{t}\sim O_{\theta^{z}}(\cdot\mid s_{t}),s_{t+1}\sim P_{\theta^{z}}(\cdot\mid x_{t}),(r_{t},c_{t})\sim(R_{\theta^{z}},C_{\theta^{z}})(\cdot\mid y_{t}), where θz\theta^{z} specifies appearance or task-semantic parameter changes. Camera, lighting, color, blur, and distractor shifts act primarily through OθzO_{\theta^{z}}, whereas relocating a goal or object may also change the transition dynamics and task feedback. Such semantic shifts are increasingly important for visually grounded policies, where deployment may involve diverse task-specific scenes, including different objects, workspaces, viewpoints, layouts, or instructions (Brohan et al., 2023; Pumacay et al., 2024; Fei et al., 2025), potentially inducing semantic spurious correlations as an important deployment shift (Tobin et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2023a).

3.2.2 Shift modes

A mode says how an intervention is built, and is one field of the specification tuple (source, factor, mode, magnitude, resampling rule, optional schedule, seed): the source says where the intervention enters the agent–environment interaction (Section 3.2.1), the factor says what it perturbs (e.g., gravity or friction), the magnitude says how far it departs from nominal, the resampling rule and optional schedule say how it evolves within an episode, and the seed makes its random draws reproducible. Each instantiated tuple defines one perturbation configuration. We retain the stochastic interface of Robust-Gymnasium (Gu et al., 2025), and extend it with several new modes as below:

  • •

    Stochastic. Samples signal errors or parameters from specified distributions.

  • •

    Adversarial. Computes bounded perturbations from the current states to counter the policy.

  • •

    Parametric. Applies a specified assignment, scale, offset, or translation at a severity.

  • •

    Non-stationary. Varies a mode’s severity over time or triggers intermittent disturbances.

  • •

    Composition. Stacks compatible shifts into reproducible multi-shift scenarios.

Together, these controls support both individual shift and compound shift scenarios. The appendix A.2 provides the operators, magnitudes, resampling rules, and composition procedure.

3.2.3 Expandable to advanced robotics tasks

Because a shift is fully described by its specification tuple, a new backend needs only one adapter to the simulator’s own primitives. We validate this on two deployment-oriented platforms. For Isaac Lab (Mittal et al., 2025), the adapter realizes transition, action, and latency shifts on the vectorized GPU environment and exposes a joint-limit cost channel for every method’s evaluation, so unconstrained and constrained learners are compared on one safety quantity. For a VLA policy (Intelligence et al., 2025) fine-tuned on the bimanual demonstrations (Zhang et al., 2026), the adapter injects appearance, proprioception, action, latency, and physical shifts into a closed-loop simulator.

4 Experimental Evaluation

The evaluation proceeds in three blocks over our library. Section 4.1 measures how much robust methods gain across the whole library and how that gain behaves as the shifts intensify. Section 4.2 isolates each shift source and composes them, to ask which shift source a method actually defends. Section 4.3 carries the same interface to deployment-oriented humanoid and vision–language–action (VLA) systems.

Experimental setup.

The library implements 23 algorithms: 6 standard RL references, 15 robust RL and 2 robust safe RL algorithms. The library-wide grid runs the 20 algorithms across Locomotion, Manipulation, Navigation and Vehicle Control; one robust RL and two robust safe algorithms enter on the advanced robotic tasks. Every algorithm starts from the same nominal task specification, uses its native training procedure and prescribed budget, and is then frozen and evaluated on the same shift grid. The results use five training seeds and 20 paired evaluation episodes per condition. Exact environments, perturbation configurations, and protocols are in Appendix B.

Performance metric.

For a comparable return across different tasks, we report the unclipped normalized score S⁡(R¯)=100​(R¯−Rmin)/(Rmax−Rmin)\mathrm{S}(\bar{R})=100(\bar{R}-R_{\min})/(R_{\max}-R_{\min}) as our evaluation metric, where RminR_{\min} and RmaxR_{\max} are fixed task-level reference returns shared by every method. Appendix B.1 details the metrics.

4.1 Evaluation of the algorithm library

Robust RL methods differ in their training assumptions and access to data and environments, making results from their original settings difficult to compare directly. We therefore evaluate their final policies on representative tasks to identify their capability boundaries. Our first comparison covers 20 online and offline algorithms, including 6 standard and 14 robust RL, over 220 perturbation configurations across four task families. Figure 3 shows each robust algorithm separately, while Figure 4 aggregates the same evaluation by shift levels and algorithm features to show both the robust–standard gap and feature-grouped algorithms’ gain over its base algorithms.

Robust RL helps at every shift level, but both degrade as shifts intensify.

Across all four shift levels, robust methods achieve a higher pooled normalized score than standard RL. Their advantage remains positive but narrows from +10.3+10.3 points in Q1 to +5.1+5.1 in Q4, while both groups’ scores decline as shifts intensify.

Methods that explicitly model dynamics shifts exhibit greater robustness to such shifts.

Two families explicitly target dynamics shifts: environment-centric online methods such as DR-SAC perturb the environment simulator during training, while generative offline methods such as FWM learn a generative dynamics model and train on its trajectories. These families achieve the strongest performance under the controlled dynamic shifts within their respective online and offline settings. Overall, robustness gains reflect both the robust methods and the strength of the base learner.

4.2 Evaluation under diverse deployment shifts

We evaluate method-specific robustness through individual shift source sweeps across 44 perturbation configurations and reference-derived compound shifts. The former cover multiple perturbation modes. For the latter, Hopper adapts the coupled physical, actuation, force, and delay factors of OmniH2O (He et al., 2024), while Pusher adapts the dynamics, observation, and control-rate factors of Peng et al. (2018), with goal displacement labeled separately. Appendix B.2 details the individual and the compound shift scenarios.

Claimed target shifts do not fully predict empirical strengths.

Figure 5 shows DR-SAC leads dynamics and execution latency, while ATLA-SA-PPO leads observation and action; offline leaders vary across shift sources. A method’s intended target shift therefore does not uniquely determine where it performs best. The measured ranking is also conditional on the task, shift mode and specific perturbation used to instantiate each shift.

Online robust methods generally achieve larger gains over their base algorithms than offline robust methods.

Figure 7 shows that online methods can produce large gains on most shift sources, whereas most offline differences remain close to their base algorithms. The smaller offline increments may partly reflect limited coverage of the tested perturbation modes in fixed datasets. Because offline RL relies on fixed data, methods often use conservative updates to limit value overestimation which potentially constrains robustness gains.

Dynamic shifts cause the largest performance drops, while the next most impactful shift varies by task.

We test our strongest online (ATLA-SA-PPO) and offline robust (RORL) algorithms under compound shifts. Figure 7 shows that dynamic dominate both scenarios. Dynamic shift is the most damaging shift source in the two tasks, while the next most damaging differs by task. Locomotion loses about two-thirds of its score to latency, because delayed action on a balancing gait is a fall rather than a slower trajectory, while semantic shift on manipulation costs a quarter, because it moves the goal of the policy. Therefore, a sim-to-real design must identify which shift is core to its task. Composition is worse than any of its parts, making both algorithms drop below half of nominal. This indicates the poor capability of algorithms in complex, multi-shift environments.

4.3 Extension to advanced robotic tasks

We extend the benchmark from standard control to advanced robotics tasks, attaching the same disruptor interface through task-specific adapters, covering a high-dimensional humanoid, a contact-rich manipulator and a VLA control task.

Robust safe methods can ensure both performance and constraint satisfaction under shifts.

We compare PPO, DR-PPO (Schwarke et al., 2025) and ATLA-PPO against the robust safe methods RAMU-PPO and SPiDR-PPO on Unitree G1 locomotion and Franka drawer manipulation in Isaac Lab (Mittal et al., 2025). Figure 8 shows the two highest-scoring policies on G1 survive about a quarter under action delay; while on the drawer DR-PPO matches SPiDR-PPO’s 99.6%99.6\% performance with 0%0\% of its episodes inside the joint-limit cost budget against SPiDR-PPO’s 84%84\%. The results indicate that only robust safe methods especially SPiDR-PPO, keep both metrics high on both tasks, so a higher performance is not the evidence that a method is ready for sim-to-real deployment.

Performance sensitivity differs sharply across shift sources, with semantic shifts more impactful in VLA tasks.

We fine-tune π0.5\pi_{0.5} on the insert-mouse-battery task (Figure 11) and drive it under eight shift factors. At the largest measured level the policy still remains 0.950.95 of its nominal performance under gravity but only 0.330.33 under image blur. Blur at its largest level moves only 13% of the image but drops the policy to a third of nominal, while image brightness moves the same frames at seven times and costs almost nothing. Semantic shift is a core shift source which affects more than physical shifts since a clear scene is the base of the action chunk.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we introduce RobustRLlib, an algorithm-centric library and evaluation platform for robust RL under deployment shifts. It integrates 17 robust RL algorithms with 6 standard RL baselines, organized by algorithm feature, claimed target shift, and base algorithm. A shared interface evaluates MDP-element shifts alongside control-loop latency and task semantics through individual and compound shift scenarios and extends to advanced robotics tasks. Under a unified evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations, robust methods as a group outperform standard RL references. Individual and compound shift evaluations further reveal each algorithmic feature’s strengths and capability boundaries. Therefore, RobustRLlib provides a platform to support more comprehensive evaluation and guide the design of future robust RL methods.

Appendix A Benchmark construction

A.1 Benchmark Comparison

Table 2 compares evaluated capabilities with 6 related benchmarks. Algorithm counts include robust and robust safe RL method. Shift entries require reported evaluations, whereas task expansion denotes a documented interface for adding task backends. These criteria distinguish a benchmark’s demonstrated scope from its potential extensibility.

The compared systems standardize different parts of robust RL evaluation. RLlib provides general-purpose algorithm infrastructure; RRLS and ODRL compare methods primarily under dynamics-related uncertainty (Liang et al., 2018; Zouitine et al., 2024; Lyu et al., 2024). Robust-Gymnasium offers broad disrupted environments, including semantic tasks, while the RWRL Suite evaluates practical stressors such as latency and their combination (Gu et al., 2025; Dulac-Arnold et al., 2020). RoAd-RL focuses on observation attacks and inference-time defenses (Mohan et al., 2026). Rather than claiming these capabilities individually as new, RobustRLlib combines a structured robust online, offline, and safe RL library with isolated and composed shift evaluations under a shared protocol. Its task-specific adapters further demonstrate how the evaluation methodology extends from standard control to advanced robotics tasks such as Isaac Lab and a VLA pipeline.

A.2 Disruptor toolbox: shift modes, operators and implementations

A perturbation configuration is specified by (source, factor, mode, magnitude, resampling rule, optional schedule, seed). The source identifies where the intervention enters the agent–environment interaction (Section 3.2), the factor names the perturbed quantity (e.g., gravity, friction, or an observation channel), the mode specifies how the intervention is constructed, and the magnitude sets how far it departs from nominal in the operator’s natural units. The resampling rule determines whether a value is redrawn at each step, held for an episode, or fixed. The optional schedule controls when the intervention is active and how its magnitude evolves, while the seed makes stochastic draws reproducible. The main text summarizes five shift modes; here we detail their source-specific modes, indexed in Table 3.

A.2.1 Shift source: Latency

We treat latency as a composable deployment-shift source within this unified robust RL evaluation framework. Specifically, we expose observation delay, action delay, and control-period variation through o~t=ℐ(ℋt,t−δo),a~t=at−δa,st+1∼P0(κt)(⋅∣st,a~t)\tilde{o}_{t}=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{H}_{t},t-\delta_{o}),\tilde{a}_{t}=a_{t-\delta_{a}},s_{t+1}\sim P_{0}^{(\kappa_{t})}(\cdot\mid s_{t},\tilde{a}_{t}), capturing delayed sensing, delayed execution, and variable control rates, respectively. The three operators act at different points of one decision and are implemented accordingly.

  • •

    Observation latency. A timestamped history ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} is queried at t−δot-\delta_{o} using linear interpolation, so sub-step delays are not rounded away (Tan et al., 2018). If the requested time precedes reset, the history returns the reset observation.

  • •

    Action latency. An integer buffer executes the command from δa\delta_{a} control steps earlier, a~t=amax⁡(t−δa,0)\tilde{a}_{t}=a_{\max(t-\delta_{a},0)}, using the initial command to warm-start the buffer.

  • •

    Control-period variation. Following Peng et al. (2018), we set Δ​tt=Δ​t0+ξt\Delta t_{t}=\Delta t_{0}+\xi_{t}, where ξt∼Exp⁡(λ)\xi_{t}\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda); λ\lambda is drawn per episode and ξt\xi_{t} per decision. One command is held for κt=round⁡(Δ​tt/hsim)\kappa_{t}=\operatorname{round}(\Delta t_{t}/h_{\mathrm{sim}}) simulator substeps, changing its duration time.

A.2.2 Operator details

  • •

    Stochastic. Signal noise is redrawn per step, whereas bias persists for an episode and dynamics parameters are sampled at reset. loguniform samples in log space to balance reciprocal multipliers. Latency draws act on command buffers, timestamped observations, or action-hold duration.

  • •

    Adversarial. The observation operator searches for an input that changes the current actor’s output within radius ϵ\epsilon; it requires a differentiable feed-forward actor. The three action operators respectively oppose the chosen command, rotate a 2-D command, or suppress its goal-directed component. Commands are clipped to the action space before perturbation.

  • •

    Parametric. These operators apply a specified value rather than draw one. set handles parameters whose nominal value is zero, while translate expresses a displacement in physical units. Semantic operators change appearance or task referents.

  • •

    Non-stationary. A schedule changes the shift magnitude over time, whereas latency operators change when signals enter the control loop. push creates an intermittent event. For feedback delay, interval release sums rewards over kk steps, while shifted release delivers each reward kk steps later; both flush pending feedback at episode end.

  • •

    Composition. An ordered list specifies wrapper order explicitly. Each specification uses its own seeded random stream, making compound conditions reproducible.

Appendix B Evaluation protocol

B.1 Metrics

Normalized score.

To compare standard-control tasks with different native metrics, let R¯\bar{R} denote the mean raw task score over evaluation episodes. We report the unclipped normalized score

S⁡(R¯)=100​R¯−RminRmax−Rmin,\mathrm{S}(\bar{R})=100\frac{\bar{R}-R_{\min}}{R_{\max}-R_{\min}}, (2)

where RminR_{\min} and RmaxR_{\max} are fixed task-level reference scores shared by all methods, seeds, and shift conditions. We use published D4RL references where available and otherwise use task-defined or reference-policy anchors; all values are listed in Table 7. Normalization precedes cross-task aggregation. For the standard-control experiments, we map each task’s native metric to a common comparable scale.

Performance and safety.

We report performance and safety separately on the advanced robotic tasks. For G1, performance is PPO-reference-normalized return over five out-of-envelope conditions (Table 7), while safety is the fraction of episodes surviving the 20 s horizon under 20–80 ms action delays. For Drawer, performance is the fraction of episodes opening the drawer beyond 0.300.30 m over fourteen out-of-envelope conditions; safety is the fraction whose cumulative joint-limit cost remains below the per-episode budget of 2020. We average episodes within each training seed, then report the mean and standard deviation across seeds.

B.2 Evaluation grids

The main robust RL algorithms evaluation grid varies one shift factor at a time across online and offline tasks, grouping its non-nominal settings into four task–factor-specific shift levels (Table 4). The grid is fixed and same for every algorithm: 220220 non-nominal conditions, 110110 online and 110110 offline, plus the nominal setting of every factor. The individual shift grid instead varies intervention modes within a shift source, allowing method-level specialization to be diagnosed (Table 5). Finally, the compound grid activates physical, control, sensing, and timing factors jointly in reference-derived Hopper and Pusher tasks (Table 6). Thus, the three grids measure robustness breadth, shift-specific behavior, and robustness under interacting deployment factors, respectively.

The advanced tasks bring their own grids, and both place every method on the same conditions. On Isaac Lab the conditions are positioned relative to the reference envelope (He et al., 2024) of Tables 8 and 9: G1 has 3131 per seed, six inside that envelope, eighteen on its boundary, five beyond it, and flat and rough nominal. Drawer has 1616, two controls and fourteen beyond the reference ranges, each moving one axis while the rest keep their training randomization.

The VLA evaluation tests eight shift factors across five shift sources (Figure 9). Each factor has its own Q1–Q4 ladder, ordered outward from its nominal setting. Hardware logs place execution delay (8383 ms) and command noise (0.0200.020 rad) at Q2, so the sweep includes both milder and more severe conditions than those measured on the platform. We report the actual input change for perception and command shifts separately; the three dynamics shifts are specified in physical units.

Appendix C Benchmark tasks and datasets

In this section we present an overview of the environments the benchmark evaluates on, the control interface each of them exposes, and the offline datasets learn from. The main experiment in Section 4.1 covers locomotion, manipulation, navigation, and vehicle control; Pusher and DoorCausal provide the additional semantic-channel tests and compound-profile in Section 4.2. Table 10 gives the default interface of every task we included in our benchmark.

Offline methods learn from the fixed datasets in Table 11. We use Minari (Younis et al., 2024), including its D4RL ports (Fu et al., 2020), wherever a corresponding dataset is available; only for LunarLander do we collect our own dataset.

Advanced robotic tasks.

These tasks test robust safe algorithms and show our interface extensibility meanwhile. In Isaac Lab (Mittal et al., 2025), Unitree G1 (Figure 10) locomotion measures return and survival under delay, and Franka drawer manipulation measures success and joint-limit cost under physical shifts. The VLA task (Figure 11) fine-tunes π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Intelligence et al., 2025) on expert demonstrations for the bimanual insert-mouse-battery task from the RSS 2026 post-training challenge (Zhang et al., 2026), then evaluates perception and execution shifts through camera and robot-state interfaces.

Appendix D Algorithms

The library holds six standard RL baselines without any robust design, thirteen robust RL algorithms, and two robust safe algorithms. They are organized by the taxonomy of Section 3.1.

D.1 Offline algorithms

D.1.1 Standard RL baselines.

IQL

IQL (Kostrikov et al., 2021) avoids querying out-of-distribution actions altogether: a value function is fitted to the critic by expectile regression, the twin critics bootstrap from that value function, and the actor is extracted by advantage-weighted regression.

TD3+BC

TD3+BC (Fujimoto and Gu, 2021) adds a behavior-cloning term to the TD3 actor loss and normalizes states. The term is balanced against the critic by dividing by the mean absolute QQ over the batch.

MOPO

MOPO (Yu et al., 2020b) learns an ensemble dynamics model, branches short rollouts from dataset states, and penalizes the rollout reward by the model’s predicted uncertainty before running SAC on the mixture of real and model data.

SynthER

SynthER (Lu et al., 2023) fits a diffusion model to logged transitions and trains an unmodified offline learner on a much larger sample from it. We count it as data augmentation rather than a generative method: it samples individual transitions to enlarge the dataset, where FWM and PLR-PVL sample multi-step futures conditioned on the current state and turn them into critic targets.

D.1.2 Learner-centric algorithms.

RFQI

RFQI (Panaganti et al., 2022) replaces the fitted-QQ target by a worst-case Bellman backup over a total-variation uncertainty set of radius ρ\rho around the empirical transitions; the inner maximization is solved through a dual variable fitted per batch, and the actor and critic follow the release’s BCQ-style architecture.

RORL

RORL (Yang et al., 2022) makes an SAC learner conservative through smoothing: the critic and policy are regularized to vary little within an ϵ\epsilon-ball of dataset states, and QQ-values at perturbed states are penalized by the disagreement of a ten-critic ensemble.

ATLA-IQL

The offline ATLA adaptation (Zhang et al., 2021) keeps ATLA’s principle, a learned observation adversary alternated with the learner, but the adversary is trained by a differentiable objective on the critic by minimizing the minimum QQ at the policy’s action under the perturbed state since no environment is available.

D.1.3 Data-centric algorithms.

RSC-IQL

RSC-IQL (Ding et al., 2023a) applies RSC’s counterfactual rewriting to logged data where a causal mask over state dimensions is fitted from the dataset, and transitions are rewritten by permuting or perturbing the dimensions the mask marks as non-causal.

RAMBO

RAMBO (Rigter et al., 2022) augments the dataset with short rollouts from a learned dynamics ensemble and replaces the uncertainty penalty by adversarial training of the model: the ensemble is updated to lower the critic’s value of the policy’s transitions while a maximum-likelihood term keeps it close to the data.

D.1.4 Generative model.

ROMB

ROMB (Chen et al., 2025) adapts a learned world model against the policy under a constrained maximin objective: the model is pushed toward transitions that lower the policy’s value while a supervised loss keeps it on the data, and the policy is trained on rollouts from the adapted model.

FWM

FWM transfers the multi-step future modeling of Diffusion World Model (Ding et al., 2024) to a flow-matching (Lipman et al., 2022) world model: instead of a one-step bootstrap, the critic regresses an hh-step return whose future is sampled from the generative model conditioned on the current state, action and return-to-go. Writing x1x_{1} for a length-TT window of states and rewards and x0∼𝒩⁡(0,I)x_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), the diffusion model’s denoising objective becomes a regression onto the straight-line velocity of the linear path xt=(1−t)​x0+t​x1x_{t}=(1-t)\,x_{0}+t\,x_{1},

ℒ=𝔼t∼𝒰⁡[0,1],x0,(x1,c,g)​∥vθ​(xt,t,c,g)−(x1−x0)∥22,\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1],\,x_{0},\,(x_{1},c,g)}\big\lVert v_{\theta}(x_{t},t,c,g)-(x_{1}-x_{0})\big\rVert_{2}^{2}, (3)

with cc the current state and action and gg the return-to-go, dropped with probability 0.20.2 so one network carries both the conditional and the unconditional velocity. Sampling then replaces the reverse diffusion chain by an ODE integrated from t=0t=0 to t=1t=1 in N=5N=5 midpoint steps on the guidance-mixed velocity:

v~θ=wvθ(⋅∣c,g)+(1−w)vθ(⋅∣∅),w=2.0.\tilde{v}_{\theta}=w\,v_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c,g)+(1-w)\,v_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\varnothing),\qquad w=2.0. (4)
PLR-PVL

PLR-PVL (Berdica et al., 2024) trains a collection of world models consistent with the offline data, treats each as a level in the sense of unsupervised environment design, and prioritizes them during policy learning by the value loss they induce. We adapt the method by replacing their world model with the flow-matching model of  equation 3: the ensemble is KK flow models differing only in training seed, each proposing one hh-step future for the same conditioning, and the critic target is taken per sample from the model whose rollout carries the largest positive value loss,

k⋆=arg⁡maxk​1h​∑t=1hmax⁡(δt(k), 0),k^{\star}=\arg\max_{k}\;\frac{1}{h}\sum_{t=1}^{h}\max\!\big(\delta^{(k)}_{t},\,0\big), (5)

where δt(k)\delta^{(k)}_{t} is the GAE-λ\lambda residual of the current critic along the kk-th rollout.

D.2 Online algorithms

D.2.1 Standard RL baselines.

SAC

SAC (Haarnoja et al., 2018) is the off-policy reference: twin critics with a clipped double-QQ target and a stochastic actor whose objective adds an entropy bonus with automatically tuned temperature.

PPO

PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) is the on-policy reference: a clipped probability-ratio surrogate on trajectories from the current policy, with generalized advantage estimation.

TRPO

TRPO (Schulman et al., 2015) replaces PPO’s clipped surrogate by an explicit KL trust region solved with conjugate gradients. It appears only as the base of RARL-TRPO.

D.2.2 Learner-centric algorithms

ATLA

ATLA (Zhang et al., 2021) trains a policy against an optimal observation adversary in the state-adversarial MDP (Zhang et al., 2020): the adversary is itself an RL agent that outputs a bounded perturbation of the observation, is rewarded by the protagonist’s negative return, and is updated in alternation with the protagonist.

ATLA-SA

ATLA-SA (Zhang et al., 2021) adds the SA-PPO regularizer (Zhang et al., 2020) to ATLA: a KL penalty between the policy at a state and at the worst-case neighbor found by stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, and a recurrent (LSTM) policy with a 100-step history so that the agent can infer a persistent perturbation from context.

RSC

RSC (Ding et al., 2023a) learns a causal graph and dynamics model over the state variables from replayed experience, then generates counterfactual transitions by intervening on the variables the graph marks as non-causal for the reward. Mixing these into replay removes the spurious correlations a policy would otherwise exploit.

D.2.3 Environment-centric algorithms.

RARL

RARL (Pinto et al., 2017) casts robustness as a two-player zero-sum game: an adversary applies bounded external forces to the robot and is trained to minimize the protagonist’s return, and the two are updated in alternating blocks. We implement RARL-PPO and RARL-TRPO in our library.

DR

Domain randomization (Tobin et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2018) samples simulator parameters from fixed ranges at every episode so that the policy meets a distribution of dynamics during training. We implement DR-PPO and DR-SAC in our library.

D.2.4 Robust safe methods.

RAMU

RAMU (Queeney and Benosman, 2023) applies a risk measure over sampled next-state perturbations to both the reward and the cost targets; the original is defined for TD learners, and the row reported here is a PPO adaptation that applies the same transform to PPO’s value targets.

SPiDR

SPiDR (As et al., 2026) trains a constrained policy under domain randomization and adds a pessimistic cost penalty proportional to the disagreement of next-state predictions across sampled dynamics; it runs with the authors’ solver and a joint-limit cost budget.

Appendix E Training Settings

E.1 Training protocol

We train each method with five independent seeds to its budget in Table 14. Unless otherwise noted, we freeze the final checkpoint and evaluate each policy for 20 episodes per condition using the same evaluation seed. RFQI retains its native best-checkpoint selection rule.

Our default protocol trains on the nominal task and introduces shifts only when evaluating the frozen policy. Reward shift and latency delivery are exceptions: they affect learning feedback but cannot alter the actions of a frozen policy. We therefore apply these shifts during training and evaluate the resulting policies on the nominal task.

The Isaac Lab and VLA studies are reported under their own protocol, and the departures are the following. Isaac Lab tasks use three training seeds and score 128128 episodes per condition. They match the retained primary training interactions within each task to the budget in Table 15. The five methods share one base learner, so the comparison is between mechanisms rather than between releases. And they do not hold the shift grid out from training: PPO and RAMU-PPO train on the nominal specification, whereas DR-PPO, ATLA-PPO and SPiDR-PPO each train inside a randomization envelope. Table 8 and Table 9 show the envelopes applied in our benchmark, which is transferred from a humanoid sim-to-real pipeline (He et al., 2024). The VLA task finetunes a single π0.5\pi_{0.5} model on demonstrations, and evaluated by joint-space tracking against the recorded demonstration.

E.2 Training budget alignment

This part presents our training budget and provides the evidence of our training protocol alignment. We train SAC-based algorithms for 1M environment steps and PPO-based algorithms for 2M steps, consistent with commonly used training budgets (Raffin and Stulp, 2020). This asymmetric budget accounts for PPO’s lower sample efficiency: as an on-policy method, PPO generally requires more environment interactions to reach a comparable level of training maturity. Figure 12 shows that the additional PPO steps provide meaningful learning progress.

However, more environment steps do not imply a larger computational budget. On Walker2d, PPO at 2M steps requires only 0.80±0.290.80\pm 0.29 hours, compared with 1.60±0.031.60\pm 0.03 hours for SAC at 1M steps on H100 GPUs (Table 12). Thus, the 2M-step PPO budget compensates for its lower sample efficiency without giving it an advantage in wall-clock compute.

For ATLA and ATLA-SA, their official configuration remains unchanged, which is about 5M protagonist steps rather than the 2M the other PPO rows use. The asymmetry is also the one the ATLA paper itself reports under: its released configurations give vanilla PPO and SA-PPO 976 iterations of the same 2048-step rollout, i.e. the same 2M our PPO row uses, against 2441 for ATLA and ATLA-SA. Our PPO-versus-ATLA comparison therefore reproduces the budget pairing those results were established with rather than introducing a new one. The full online training budget is in Table 14.

Taken together, the online budget is set by the base algorithm. Table 13 summarizes the resulting protocol. Methods sharing the same base algorithm are trained with the same budget, while ATLA and ATLA-SA retain their official ∼\sim5M-step configuration.

For the offline algorithms’ training budgets, Table 14 shows nine of the twelve offline columns share the same 1M-update budget. RAMBO and RORL (Rigter et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022) follow their official budgets on the tasks their releases cover and keep the 1M budget elsewhere. Thus, our MuJoCo comparisons with 1M-update references preserve native budgets. RFQI (Panaganti et al., 2022) follows its official budget and reports its own best checkpoint, because forcing it onto the common protocol would break its mechanism.

Appendix G Additional results and analysis

G.1 Analysis of robust methods’ gains

Figure 4 reports two gains for each algorithmic feature family. The darker column is the base-relative gain: each method with a matched base learner is compared with that base algorithm under the same conditions, and the differences are averaged within the family. Standalone recipes without a matched reference learner, including RFQI, RORL, and RAMBO, are excluded; the number of included methods is reported as nn in Table 41. The lighter column is the standard-pool gain: the full family’s mean minus the mean of all six Standard RL references. It therefore reflects both the robustness mechanism and the strength of its underlying learner.

Brackets denote 95% seed-level stratified bootstrap intervals from 10,00010{,}000 replicates. Each training seed contributes its mean over 20 evaluation episodes, and seeds are resampled within each (method, task) stratum, with the same draw reused across all conditions of that task. Methods and base algorithms are separate runs and are resampled independently.

The two different comparisons indicate that both online families retain positive base-relative gains (+5.5+5.5 and +6.6+6.6), whereas offline gains are smaller. The generative family offers the cleanest comparison: all three methods use IQL, yielding a +9.8+9.8 gain over the standard pool but +2.5+2.5 over IQL. Its aggregate advantage thus reflects both the added mechanism and a strong base algorithm, while fixed-data coverage may limit the incremental benefit available offline.

G.2 Analysis of task capability: On-policy vs Off-policy

On-policy methods update a policy using trajectories collected by that policy or a recent version of it, as in PPO (Schulman et al., 2017). Off-policy methods can also learn from data generated by earlier or different policies, often through experience replay, as in SAC (Haarnoja et al., 2018). This distinction concerns which data can be used for an update.

Figure 13 shows that the evaluated off-policy methods generally achieve higher scores on the MuJoCo locomotion tasks, while on-policy methods are stronger on PointMaze-UMaze and CarRace. In locomotion, frequent reward feedback allows replay-based learners to reuse informative transitions across many updates, which may contribute to the off-policy methods’ advantage. PointMaze requires discovering goal-reaching trajectories, while CarRacing couples control with visual input; updates from recent on-policy rollouts may be more useful in these settings.

G.3 Results of advanced robotic tasks

Figure 14 indicates that across the Isaac Lab tasks, SPiDR-PPO most consistently balances performance and safety: it maintains high success while satisfying the cost budget on Drawer, and leads on both return and survival under G1 action delays. These results show why high return alone is insufficient for sim-to-real evaluation. Robust-safe methods must be assessed for constraint satisfaction alongside task performance.

G.4 Supplementary results

Figures 15-17 show our complete comparison on 220 different configurations across 4 task families in Section 4.1. Figures 19 and 20 show our full shift-isolated evaluation on 44 distinct perturbation configurations. Figure 21 further shows full results on 9 perturbation configurations including compound-shifts scenario.
